newsitem.title: USA: US exchanges want stronger warehouse oversight.
newsitem.headline: US exchanges want stronger warehouse oversight.

text.p: Major U.S. commodity exchanges asked senators Tuesday for tougher rules on foreign contracts that have U.S. delivery points and cited the Sumitomo Corp scandal as justification for more U.S. oversight.

The Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange took a slightly different stance. While it joined the other exchanges in saying legislation on the issue was not strong enough, the CSCE warned against any steps that might spark retaliation against U.S.-originated contracts.

The CSCE said it was alone among U.S. exchanges in trading in commodities mostly grown outside the United States. Delivery under its biggest contract -- sugar -- must be made in foreign countries of origin.

A Senate bill to modify the Commodity Exchange Act would direct the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to consult with overseas regulators for assurances against adverse effects on U.S. markets from establishment of U.S. delivery points. The bill also would give CFTC authority to obtain information from the warehouses about transactions and dealings in the market.

In a joint statement, the seven major exchanges said the bill "simply does not go far enough to addresss the risks." Foreign regulators might not put appropriate safeguards in place or might refuse to cooperate, they said, leaving the potential that a problem would be recognized but no solution offered.

Daniel Rappaport, chairman of the New York Mercantile Exchange, told the Senate Agriculture Committee that fears of retaliation were irrational. He said the Sumitomo scandal, in which copper prices crashed following revelations of improper trading, showed the need for a sound regulatory regime.
COMEX suggested an amendment giving CFTC the power to require marketing of foreign contracts to be consistent with CFTC rules if they have U.S. delivery points.
Copper trading is dominated by the London Metal Exchange, which opened U.S. warehouses in the past couple of years. COMEX also trades a copper contract.

Under CFTC rules, a great deal of information was available to the public about ownership and positions in COMEX-traded copper, the exchanges said in their statement. "Parallel informaton was not available for LME transactions."
